newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Old enemies India, Pakistan edge towards talks.
newsitem.headline: Old enemies India, Pakistan edge towards talks.

text.p: Arch-rivals India and Pakistan are preparing warily to resume long-stalled talks, but their dispute over Kashmir makes an early breakthrough unlikely.

"I don't think we should expect much immediately," said Brahma Chellaney, defence analyst at the Centre for Policy Research in New Delhi. "Negotiations are going to be slow and painfully long. We should not expect a conclusion soon."
Foreign ministry-level talks collapsed in January 1994 because of deep disagreements over Kashmir, which sparked two of the three wars Pakistan and India have fought since independence in 1947.
The advent to power of Pakistan's new Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif, convincing winner of February 3 elections, has generated fresh hope that the two countries can revive the dialogue.

Sharif proposed on Thursday that he and Indian Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda meet after preparatory talks by senior officials. In India a senior official said his government would respond "constructively" to Pakistan's offer.
Sharif said in a letter to Deve Gowda that top foreign ministry officials should meet in March to "prepare the ground for meaningful discussions" between the two prime ministers.
Deve Gowda has told Sharif he wants talks on a wide range of issues and has not excluded discussion of the Himalayan region of Jammu and Kashmir, which India considers its territory.
Pakistan, which controls a third of Kashmir, wants mainly Moslem Kashmiris to be allowed to vote under U.N. supervision whether to join Islamic Pakistan or Hindu-majority India.
India maintains that the status of Kashmir is not negotiable and at most wants to keep the issue on the back-burner.
"If India and Pakistan want to normalise relations, they should go for a dialogue keeping aside the Kashmir issue as it is most difficult to resolve," said Chellaney.

Sharif's letter to Deve Gowda reiterated Islamabad's insistence that Kashmir be on the agenda. "I hope you will agree with me that without some progress on the core issue of Jammu and Kashmir, it will be difficult to initiate meaningful cooperation in economic and cultural fields," he wrote.
He said he shared Deve Gowda's belief that as the two nations neared the 50th anniversary of their independence, there was an historic opportunity to deal with outstanding disputes.
For Pakistan, an Indian refusal to discuss Kashmir would effectively block progress on other bilateral issues.
A U.S. official suggested on Wednesday that Kashmir could be placed on the agenda, but not necessarily at the top.
"It is up to the two countries to decide how they fit Kashmir into the equation," Assistant Secretary of State Robin Raphel was reported as telling a seminar in Washington.

"It may be that India and Pakistan can get together and come up with some kind of negotiating process whereby the political status of Kashmir is not first on the agenda, but rather Siachen is first and trade is second," Raphel was quoted as saying.

For more than a decade, Pakistani and Indian troops have been locked in a confrontation on the icy peaks of the Siachen Glacier, the world's highest-altitude battlefield. Previous attempts to agree mutual troop pullbacks have failed.
Siachen, near the Chinese border, lies at the northern end of the Line of Control, or ceasefire line, dividing Kashmir.

Some Pakistani commentators say that even if Islamabad ignores prodding from the West to mend its fences with India, it should pay heed to advice from China, a longstanding ally now seeking better ties with India and other South Asian countries.
Chinese President Jiang Zemin said during a visit to Islamabad in December that regional countries should consider laying their thorniest disputes aside to reduce tension.
"If certain issues cannot be resolved for the time being, they may be shelved temporarily so that they will not affect the normal state-to-state relations," he said.
Sharif, in the past considered a hard-liner on Kashmir, knows that his political opponents will seize on any apparent concession to India to accuse him of betraying a sacred cause.

Qazi Hussain Ahmad, chief of the religious Jamaat-i-Islami party, which backs the Hizb-ul-Mujahideen Kashmiri guerrilla group, has said India must recognise Kashmir as disputed territory before Pakistan agrees to any talks with New Delhi.

"Kashmir, Pakistan's jugular vein, has been under Indian occupation for the past 50 years and unless it is liberated there is no point for the government to celebrate the golden jubilee of Pakistan's independence or have talks with India," he told a news conference on Thursday.
